list.listitem: All women with postmenopausal bleeding or older than 35 years with abnormal uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial cancer. C
Either endometrial biopsy or transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is appropriate diagnostic option. B
Treatment is primarily surgical; radiotherapy does not improve survival and chemotherapy is generally limited to women with more advanced or metastatic disease. B
Outcome is generally good for endometrial cancer while outcome is poor for uterine sarcoma. B

background.definition: Uterine cancer is a malignancy involving the uterine corpus. There are three major types of tumors: Type I endometrial carcinoma (estrogen-dependent, 90%), Type II endometrial carcinoma (estrogen independent, more aggressive, 10%), and uterine sarcoma.

list.listitem: 39,080 new cases estimated in 2007.
The mean age at diagnosis is 60 years.
Uterine sarcomas account for less than 5% of uterine cancers.
$1.8 billion direct health care costs estimated in 2004.
Uterine cancer is the most common female genital tract malignancy, affecting mostly postmenopausal women.
Fourth most common cancer in women but eighth most common cause of cancer death in women.
Exposure to unopposed estrogen (endogenous or exogenous) likely plays a role. Unknown etiology for estrogen-independent tumors. Both sequential and continuous progestin reduce this risk.

Route and dose of exogenous estrogen exposure might be important; one RCT of 14 mcg transdermal estradiol given to 208 women found that it did not cause endometrial hyperplasia or cancer after 2 years.
Genetic predisposition can occur; in hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer is the most common manifestation occurring in 20% to 60% of those affected.

A systematic review with almost 4000 cases and 50,000 controls has confirmed an increased relative risk of endometrial cancer in women with a first degree family history of either endometrial or colorectal cancer.
Prior pelvic radiation (OR = 10.0) and tamoxifen use (OR = 3.1) also increase the risk of uterine cancer.
Excessive and unopposed estrogen leads to endometrial hyperplasia; risk of progression ranging from 1.6% to 23% depending on the degree of atypia.

list.listitem: United States Preventive Services Task Force has no specific guidelines on screening for endometrial cancer and the American Cancer Society does not recommend routine screening of asymptomatic women by ultrasound or endometrial biopsy. C
Women at risk for or who have hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer should be offered yearly endometrial biopsy starting at age 35 given the known association with endometrial cancer. C
There is continued debate on the cost effectiveness of screening women with uterine cancer for Lynch syndrome which would predispose them to subsequent other malignancies.
Use of combined estrogen and progestin hormone therapy eliminates the risk of endometrial cancer from unopposed estrogen therapy. B
The effect of diet, weight loss, increased physical activity, and breastfeeding on the risk of endometrial cancer are inconsistent. B

In women with breast cancer taking tamoxifen, a levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces the likelihood of benign polyps and endometrial hyperplasia, and may reduce the likelihood of endometrial cancer. An observational study found a higher rate of complete resolution in the IUD group compared with systemic progestin (78% vs 47%, p < 0.001). B
All women with postmenopausal bleeding or older than 35 years with abnormal uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial cancer. C
TVUS is an option for evaluating women at low risk. B
Endometrial biopsy with or without saline hysterosonography should be used to evaluate women at average or increased risk. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Pale, dry, thin vaginal epithelium leading to friability

list.listitem: See .

The hallmark of endometrial cancer is abnormal uterine bleeding in an otherwise asymptomatic woman; some women present with atypical glandular cells on routine PAP smear requiring further evaluation. Any postmenopausal bleeding is especially worrisome.
Women considered at higher risk for endometrial cancer include those with 1 or more risk factors (eg, family history, older age, use of menopausal estrogen alone or tamoxifen, obesity).

In a group of 456 patients with recurrent abnormal uterine bleeding, risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia or cancer included: age 45 years or older (OR 2.9), a history of endometrial polyps (OR 3.7), nulliparity (OR 3.5), and less than 12 months between sampling (OR 2.4).
A diagnosis of endometrial cancer or uterine sarcoma is generally made following endometrial biopsy with histologic confirmation.

The initial approach to women suspected of having uterine cancer is either endometrial biopsy or TVUS. A meta-analysis of 11 studies comparing endometrial biopsy to dilation and curettage (D&C) found that outpatient endometrial biopsy was highly accurate.Endometrial biopsy is also quicker, less invasive, and much less expensive than D&C.

TVUS is a useful test for detection of endometrial cancer, hyperplasia, or polyp. Measurement of the endometrial stripe has comparable negative predictive value to endometrial sampling (~0.1) and is usually less painful and less expensive.However, approximately 4% of women with cancer will be missed and about half of the women who test positive by ultrasound will have negative D&C. In addition, the lower limit of normal endometrial stripe thickness varies between centers; therefore, local norms should be considered when interpreting endometrial stripe thickness on TVUS. Endometrial stripe thickness is less reliable in premenopausal women, in postmenopausal women on hormone therapy, and in diabetic postmenopausal women.

Tests usually reserved for women with a thick endometrial stripe or nondiagnostic biopsy include saline hysterosonography and hysteroscopy. A large meta-analysis suggests saline hysterosonography is accurate, less invasive, and less expensive than hysteroscopy but does not allow treatment at the time of testing.Hysteroscopy (without biopsy) is very accurate at diagnosing endometrial cancer in women with abnormal vaginal bleeding (LR+ 60.9). It is more accurate in postmenopausal women.
CT scan is specific but relatively insensitive for the detection of nodal metastases. PET scanning can increase the diagnostic accuracy over CT alone in high risk patients.
See Figure 2 in chapter on Abnormal Uterine Bleeding for a suggested approach to evaluation.
Endometrial biopsy is the recommended initial test; ultrasound is an option for low-risk women, and in that group endometrial thickness less than 5 mm makes malignancy extremely unlikely.
First-line treatment for most women is surgical (total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy [TAH-BSO]) which is both therapeutic and prognostic (allows staging). B
Women who are not surgical candidates or elect not to have surgery may benefit from radiotherapy or a progestin. B
The mainstay of treatment for women with endometrial cancer is TAH-BSO, pelvic and paraaortic lymph node resection, and pelvic washings (serving as both a therapeutic and prognostic measure).

A Cochrane review including eight trials and 3644 patients with early stage endometrial cancer found similar disease free and overall survival for use of laparoscopic surgery compared to laparotomy with benefit of reduced morbidity.

A recent systematic review of over 2,500 patients found equivalent disease free and overall survival for patients receiving minimally invasive surgery compared to open surgery for high risk endometrial cancer.
There is no evidence for complete lymphadenectomy in endometrial cancer, based on a Cochrane review including two trials and 1945 patients.
Assessment of sentinel lymph node biopsy in high grade endometrial disease suggests this may be useful.

Although robotic surgery has been reported effective in controlled clinical trials, this is an evolving area of research. One small RCT suggests that robotic surgery is faster with no negative impact on outcomes. Long-term (10 year) follow-up of the 97 patients in this study found no clinically important differences between groups.

A randomised trial of an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol in a group of women undergoing gyanecologic surgery demonstrated shortened hospital stay and reduced complication rate in those with the ERAS protocol.
Only a physical examination and CXR are required for preoperative staging in patients with type 1, Grade 1 endometrial cancer.
There is some evidence to support fluids and hyaluronic acid washings intraoperatively to prevent adhesions.

While it reduces the risk of locoregional recurrence in some subgroups, there is no evidence that adjunctive radiotherapy following surgery reduces the risk of death in women with Stage I endometrial cancer.

A systematic review of 24 trials with nearly 5000 patients found that combined chemotherapy and radiation therapy for patients with locally advanced uterine cancer improves survival, especially in patients with stage I or II disease. The studies were somewhat heterogeneous, though. A new large RCT (n=813) addressing the addition of radiation to chemotherapy in stage III/IV disease post-operatively determined that there was no benefit from adjuvant radiation.Modern chemotherapy regimens based on platinum improved survival in women with endometrial cancer, regardless of whether they were used with or without radiation (relative risk reduction 25%, NNT = 25 for overall survival).

The optimal chemotherapeutic regimen for women with advanced, metastatic, or recurrent endometrial carcinoma is unclear. A systematic review of 11 RCTs with over 2000 women found support for paclitaxel and platinum. There was a significant benefit regarding progression free survival (HR 0.82; 95% CI, 0.74-0.90) and increased survival (HR 0.86; 95% CI, 0.77-0.96) for the comparison of "more" chemotherapy with "less" or none.

Previously there has been no standard therapy option for patients relapsing following platinum failure. A trial of 827 patients randomised between further chemotherapy for this group versus the combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab immunotherapy has established a clear survival benefit for lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab, with median survival 17.4 months compared to 12 months for chemotherapy.

A trial randomized 816 patients with advanced stage III, IVA, IVB or recurrent disease to pembrolizumab or placeo plus standard chemotherapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. At 12 months progression free survival was higher in the pembrolizumab group (74% vs 38%, p < 0.001, NNT = 3). Median progression free survival was 13.1 months with pembrolizumab compared to 8.7 months with carboplatin/paclitaxel alone.

A systematic review of seven studies with 4556 patients found that adjunctive therapy with progestins does not improve outcome in endometrial cancer. In a small series of 75 women, use of hormone therapy after definitive treatment for endometrial cancer did not appear to increase the risk of recurrence.

In the setting of advanced endometrial cancer, a systematic review similarly found no survival benefit for hormone therapy although the six studies included were underpowered and there was no quality of life data.

Dostarlimab is an immune-checkpoint inhibitor targetting PCD 1. A trial randomized 494 patients with stage III or IV endometrial cancer or first recurrence of endometrial cancer to dostarlimab 500 mg or placebo plus carboplatin and paclitaxel. Overall survival was greater in the dostarlimab group (71.3% vs 56%, p < 0.05, NNT = 7).
Systematic review with 26 studies and 1639 patients has shown there may in fact be a role for progestin therapy in advanced and recurrent disease with increased response rates compared to control.

For women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia and low-grade endometrial cancer who wish to maintain fertility, treatment with progestins and close clinical follow-up to document the response is an option.

For women with intraepithelial neoplasia, a meta-analysis of studies comparing oral progestin therapy with IUD containing progestin demonstrated higher complete response rate with IUD (95% vs 82%) but a lower rate of subsequent pregnancy (35% vs 50%).
Prognosis is good for most patients with an overall 5-year survival rate of more than 80%; prognosis for uterine sarcoma is worse. B

Usual follow-up involves pelvic examination every 3 to 4 months for 2 to 3 years and then twice annually. While ultrasound, CA-125, and CT scan are often used in follow-up evidence of benefit is lacking. C

A study of follow-up scheduling in patients with early stage disease found that patient-initiated follow-up compared to hospital set scheduled follow-up had no negative impact on fear of recurrence or quality of life.

Prognosis for endometrial carcinoma and uterine sarcoma is based primarily on surgical staging (). The overall 5-year survival rate for endometrial carcinoma ranges from more than 80% for Stage I disease to less than 20% for Stage IV disease.
Prognosis for uterine sarcoma is less favorable with an overall 5-year survival rate of 50% for stage I disease, and 0% to 20% for all other stages.
Even in light of improved survival rates, an estimated 7400 women die each year from endometrial cancer.
For incompletely understood reasons, black women tend to fare worse than white women with a 5-year survival rate for those diagnosed at age 65 or older of 53.3% and 80.8%, respectively.
It is recommended that women undergoing surgery without radiotherapy be evaluated with pelvic examinations every 3 to 4 months for 2 to 3 years, then twice yearly.
As almost 70% of recurrences are symptomatic, follow-up is often aimed at evaluation of symptoms (eg, vaginal bleeding, abdominal/pelvic pain, weight loss).

There is no evidence to support a preferred monitoring strategy, although regular follow-up of varying intervals is recommended. Monitoring can include physical examination, vaginal cytology, chest x-ray, CA-125 trending, abdominal/pelvic ultrasound and/or abdominal/pelvic CT scan.

A Danish multicentre study of patients with stage I endometrial cancer randomised participants to patient initiated follow-up or routine hospital follow-up. While patient initiated follow-up in low risk patients reduced healthcare costs, it was associated with a significant increase in fear of cancer recurrence in patients.
In one study, 34% of recurrences were found during the first year and 74% during the first 3 years; half were local recurrences.

Radiation induced cystitis has been reported as a troublesome late effect of pelvic radiotherapy. While there are many studies addressing the efficacy of non-surgical interventions for relief of symptoms, there is no good level evidence to support any individual intervention.
Primary therapeutic radiation can be considered in poor surgical candidates.
Primary therapeutic progestational treatment can be considered in women desiring to maintain fertility.
